title: Three Fingers and a Thumb

where.detail: the mill tracks north of Coldmere, across the noon ford and climbing into the hills

time: the first day on the mill tracks: the morning in the hedges, the noon halt at a brook, the afternoon climbing
last_beat: On the far side of the ford Maelis said good, and he looked back down the track toward Coldmere as he had twice that morning: hedge, a strip of sky, and nothing on the sky yet.

people.did: Hid his right hand in his coat all morning, working the last two fingers and hoping to have them back before the noon Reading; was caught at it, told they are slow for good, found the grip left to him on the stick and the oilcloth sword, said he would sooner have the fingers and would take the stop, and crossed the ford.
people.now: Walking at Hob's head up the mill tracks past the noon ford, the stick high in a new grip of three fingers and a thumb, the hills ahead and one rider somewhere behind.

facts.fact: All morning on the mill tracks he worked the last two fingers of his right hand and hid it in his coat, hoping to have them back before the noon Reading.
facts.evidence: He had until noon.

facts.fact: At the noon Reading on the mill tracks Maelis told him the two last fingers of his right hand have come back as far as they will, slow and half there, from the frost at the grate under the House.
facts.evidence: They've come back as far as they'll come. Slow, and half there.

facts.fact: He found the grip left to him: the stick and the sword held high in the thumb and the first two fingers, the two slack ones laid along the wood.
facts.evidence: three fingers and a thumb

facts.fact: He said he would sooner have the fingers, and that he would take the stop.
facts.evidence: I'd sooner have the fingers.

facts.fact: He told Maelis he would have taken the hard word about the knee instead, and she said he had been waiting for it since the river.
facts.evidence: I'd have taken that about the knee,

facts.fact: He said there is a grey in Coldmere he will want a rein for in the spring.
facts.evidence: There's a grey in Coldmere I'll want a rein for in the spring.

people.did: Read the Knots at the noon halt a week after the Steps, then held out her hand for the right one she had watched him hide since the third gate, told him plainly what the frost had kept, unwrapped the sword for him to try the grip, and said good when he crossed the ford.
people.now: Walking behind the cart up the mill tracks with her roll on the north shoulder, the oilcloth sword back under the salt.

facts.fact: She read the Knots at the noon halt, a week after the Steps, and said the knee was walking and to walk it till she said.
facts.evidence: It's walking. Walk it. Till I say.

facts.fact: She had seen him hide his hand in his coat at the third gate and let him all morning, then told him he would do better hiding a limp.
facts.evidence: You'd do better hiding a limp,

facts.fact: She told him plainly that the frost had kept his two last fingers and would not dress it, because a Mender who lies to a patient buries him.
facts.evidence: A Mender who lies to a patient buries him.

facts.fact: She said a rein is two fingers' work, and to ask her about a saddle in the spring and not before.
facts.evidence: Ask me about a saddle in the spring, and not before.

facts.fact: She watched him cross the slab at the ford in the new grip and said good.
facts.evidence: "Good," said Maelis.

people.did: Took the frost drops on the tailboard, told Wren every mill track is the same track, and set the Captain's hand higher on the hilt: the bind is three fingers and a thumb, and two lost fingers are an argument finished.
people.now: On the tailboard going up the mill tracks, with a lesson over a wall still owed from the Coldmere well.

facts.fact: He told Darrow the bind lives in the thumb and the first two fingers and that the Seated Blade never had a use for his little finger, and set his hand higher on the hilt.
facts.evidence: The bind's in the first two and the thumb.

facts.fact: He said he had waited since he was thirty for a man with the right hand for the Seated Blade.
facts.evidence: I've been waiting to say that since I was thirty.

people.did: Counted the Captain's working fingers at eight and filed Ser Hollis's legs under furniture.
people.now: In the cart among the sacks with the ledger open, the Captain's fingers counted.

facts.fact: She counted the Captain's working fingers at eight, and keeps Ser Hollis's legs in her ledger under furniture.
facts.evidence: Fingers that work: eight,

people.did: Drove the mill tracks all morning with the rag still in her bell and the box quiet, stopped and moved the oxen with her grandmother's word, and spoke to nobody else.
people.now: Driving the mill tracks north past the ford, the rag still in her bell, her words for the oxen only.

facts.fact: On the first day up the mill tracks the first of her voice Darrow had was for the oxen at the noon ford, and she spoke to nobody else all day.
facts.evidence: the first of her voice Darrow had had all day, and it was for Hob and Dun and nobody else

people.did: Rode in the cart with the sacks.
people.now: In the cart with the sacks, going north.

codex.name: The mill tracks
codex.text: The quiet road north out of Coldmere: two ruts and a crown of frozen grass between hedges higher than a cart, climbing into the hill country toward the mills; nothing had been along it since the frost but a fox. On the first day it comes down at noon to a brook off the hills with a slab for feet and a ford for wheels (Ch 5 Choice; Ch 6 Sc 1).

codex.name: Darrow's right hand
codex.text: The last two fingers are slow and half there since the frost at the kennel grate, and Maelis told him at a Reading on the mill tracks that they have come back as far as they will. He holds the stick and a sword high now, in the thumb and the first two fingers, with the other two laid along the wood; the point stops where the wrist stops (Ch 6 Sc 1).

fired.evidence: the first of her voice Darrow had had all day, and it was for Hob and Dun and nobody else
They've come back as far as they'll come. Slow, and half there.

now.against: One rider somewhere behind them, and a quiet road north into the hills.

title: Not the Carter

where.detail: on the box of Rae's cart, climbing the mill tracks north in the afternoon

time: the afternoon of the first day on the mill tracks
last_beat: Rae set him a term on the box: next fork, he says why first, out loud, and she will say aye or not. From the tailboard Hollis asked if that was the end of it, so he could complain about the hedge down his collar.

people.did: Climbed onto the box and asked Rae straight out whether she was still angry about the river road; heard her answer, gave her the true reason he chose north, and took her term for the next fork.
people.now: On the box beside Rae, climbing the mill tracks north, his word given to say why first at the next fork.

facts.fact: He told Rae he chose the north road partly so the grey cloaks would not ask her about her cart again, having watched one question her across the water.
facts.evidence: I'd not have you asked again.

facts.fact: He owned that he had decided for her at the fork without saying so, and agreed that at the next fork he will say why first.
facts.evidence: "Next fork. Why first."

people.did: Told him she was still angry about the river road, some of her: she knows its farms and drove past them with her bell stopped; then told him the part she had chewed on since the fork, that she had been glad when he chose north for his own.
people.now: Driving the mill tracks north with Darrow beside her on the box, the rag still in her bell, her term set for the next fork.

facts.fact: She has carted salt to the farms down the river road since she could hold the lines, and said she drove past the end of it with her bell stopped, like a thief.
facts.evidence: I went by them like one.

facts.fact: She told Darrow she was glad at the fork when he chose north for his own, against her carter's rule of carrying for everybody or nobody.
facts.evidence: "I was glad," she said. "At the fork. When you said north."

facts.fact: She told him she had given him the road at the fork, never the carter.
facts.evidence: I never gave you the carter.

facts.fact: She set him a term: at the next fork he says why first, out loud, and she says aye or not.
facts.evidence: You say why first. Out loud. Then I'll say aye, or I won't.

people.quote: I gave you the road. I never gave you the carter.

people.did: Sat on the tailboard with his eyes shut, heard all of it, and asked whether it was over so he could complain about the hedge down his collar.
people.now: On the tailboard going north, complaining to a mule that agrees with him.

people.did: Slept in the sacks with the ledger under her cheek.
people.now: Asleep in the cart among the sacks, the ledger for a pillow.

people.did: Walked a dozen yards behind the cart, out of earshot.
people.now: Walking behind the cart up the mill tracks.

now.against: One rider somewhere behind them, and a quiet road north into the hills.

title: Two Carts Out of One

where.detail: a camp in the lee of a field wall on the mill tracks, past a spring dip and a farm lane

time: dusk and nightfall of the first day on the mill tracks
last_beat: Darrow had counted the quarter hour on the stones and well past it and nothing came over the shoulder; at the camp wall nothing stood on the skyline, which was either good or the opposite.

people.did: Saw the rider on the skyline a mile behind and tested it by stopping, said why first at the fork and kept the mill tracks, then kept lookout on the stones and counted the quarter hour a walking horse takes to cover a mile while Rae laid the road lie.
people.now: At a camp in the lee of a field wall on the mill tracks; nothing came over the shoulder behind them, and nothing stands on the skyline.

facts.fact: At the fork by the spring he said his reason first, out loud, as he had promised Rae: the mill tracks go to a mill with people who will lie for a carter.
facts.evidence: "Why first, then."

facts.fact: He read the rider's horse as shod to go fast and held to a walk.
facts.evidence: Shod to go fast,

facts.fact: He kept lookout on the stones while Rae laid the road lie, counting the quarter hour a walking horse takes to cover a mile, and nothing came over the shoulder.
facts.evidence: A mile at a walk was a quarter of an hour.

people.did: Made the road lie: drove the loaded cart up a farm lane through the soft ground and back on the turf, then ran it lopsided through the spring-mud on a fresh line and away over the stones, so the dip shows two carts going two ways.
people.now: At the camp wall on the mill tracks, the road behind them telling a lie she made.

facts.fact: She made the dip by the spring show two carts going two ways: one heavy up a farm lane, one light over the stones.
facts.evidence: A man reading that dip sees two carts come down off the hill and go two ways.

people.quote: It's a road. Roads say what you tell them.

people.did: Counted one rider and no column, wrote Hollis's verdict in the ledger, and counted the road lie with deep respect.
people.now: At the camp wall with the ledger, two carts on the road by their tracks and one in fact.

facts.fact: She wrote in her ledger that the riders behind them were one, which is worse than forty, according to Ser Hollis.
facts.evidence: which is worse than forty, according to Ser Hollis.

facts.fact: She called Rae's road lie the best lie she had seen since she came off the mountain.
facts.evidence: That's the best lie I've seen since I came off the mountain

people.did: Named the rider the miller's man's long-legged horse, said one rider is worse than forty, and at the camp set his hat on the far side of the field wall.
people.now: At the camp wall on the mill tracks, his hat on the far side of it in the frost.

facts.fact: He said one rider is worse than forty, because one wants something particular.
facts.evidence: One wants something particular, or they'd have sent forty.

facts.fact: At the camp he set his hat crown-down in the frost on the far side of the field wall and said that's a wall.
facts.evidence: "That's a wall," said Hollis

people.did: Looked at the rider, the light and the knee, said they would want a wall tonight, and agreed a small fire would not show.
people.now: At the camp wall on the mill tracks.

people.did: Saw the rider first, from the sacks, with her hackles up and no sound.
people.now: At the camp wall on the mill tracks.

facts.fact: She saw the rider on the skyline first and made no sound.
facts.evidence: she made no sound at all

codex.name: Two carts out of one
codex.text: A carter's road lie: at a soft crossing the loaded cart is driven up a side lane deep in the mud and brought back on the turf where the ground keeps nothing, then run lopsided through the mud again on a fresh line and away over stone, so the crossing shows two carts going two ways. Rae Thorne laid one at a spring on the mill tracks: roads say what you tell them (Ch 6 Sc 2).

now.against: One rider on a long-legged horse a mile behind, keeping the distance exactly.

title: Over the Wall

where.detail: the camp wall on the mill tracks, after dark

time: nightfall of the first day on the mill tracks
last_beat: Hollis said he would be telling it clean, two in the hat in the dark and the second cleaner than the first; Darrow said that was not what happened, and Hollis said it is now.

people.did: Took Hollis's second lesson at the camp wall: threw at a hat he could not see, put the fourth stone in, and a fifth in off the top of the wall; told Hollis he had been right about the fingers.
people.now: At the camp wall on the mill tracks after dark, two stones in Hollis's hat on the far side.

facts.fact: At the camp wall he learned Overwall from Hollis, throwing at the place a stone has to come down on the far side of a wall, and put the fourth stone into a hat he could not see.
facts.evidence: There was a small sound, like a coin dropped into a purse.

facts.fact: He told Hollis he had been right about the fingers: the stone went off cleaner without them.
facts.evidence: You were right about the fingers.

facts.fact: His second stone in the dark went in off the top of the wall.
facts.evidence: "In off the wall," said Hollis.

people.did: Kept his word from the Coldmere well: taught the Captain the throw over the wall by the sound of where each stone landed, named it Overwall, and claimed the right to tell it clean.
people.now: At the camp wall after dark with a lap full of stones and a story he means to improve.

facts.fact: He taught Overwall by ear, calling each stone by where it landed on the far side of the wall: grass, wall, short, hat.
facts.evidence: Forty years of hearing where things land, Captain.

facts.fact: He named the throw Overwall: over what is in your way and down on what is behind it.
facts.evidence: That's Overwall,

facts.fact: He said he would tell it clean in every taproom from there to the landing.
facts.evidence: I'll be telling it clean, mind.

people.quote: I'm right about most things. Nobody pays me for it.

fired.evidence: "That's Overwall," said Hollis. "Over what's in your way and down on what's behind it."

now.against: One rider on a long-legged horse somewhere behind them, out of sight since the shoulder.

title: A Captain With a Stick

time: dusk and lantern-light of the second day on the mill tracks
last_beat: In the inn yard a family off the river farms asked for the loan of Hob to the village over the hill; Rae said Hob was hers to lend and the day was his, and the man waited with his cap in his hands for the cart to make up its mind.

people.now: In the inn yard at the top of the mill tracks, a family off the river farms waiting on his answer.

codex.name: The inn at the top of the mill tracks
codex.text: A hill inn where the mill tracks come up into the hill country: one low room for everything, brown with smoke, with hill people along the benches and a yard with a trough and a mounting block. A drover told its taproom of a rider on a long-legged horse who stood the room at the landing a round, drank water, and asked how far a man with a stick walks in a day (Ch 6 Sc 3).
